extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, students, and general readers interested in number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic summary and formal formulations of the abc conjecture: definitions (radical), equivalent formulations (ε-form, K_ε-form, little-o), the quality q(a,b,c), examples, consequences, known bounds, refinements, computational data, and the status of claimed proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the radical rad(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a positive integer n, the radical of n, denoted rad(n), is the product of the distinct prime factors of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: rad(16)=2, rad(17)=17, rad(18)=6, rad(1000000)=10. This definition is used throughout the statement and reformulations of the conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coprimality condition for abc triples
rubrics_metrics.description: a, b, and c are coprime positive integers with a + b = c (in this case coprimality of a, b, c implies pairwise coprimality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a + b = c any common factor of two is shared by the third; the article notes that choice of coprimality concept does not matter in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main abc conjecture (ε-finiteness formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every positive real number ε, there exist only finitely many triples (a, b, c) of coprime positive integers, with a + b = c, such that c > rad(abc)^{1+ε}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard formulation emphasized in the article; the role of ε>0 is necessary (see separate entry with explicit infinite-family examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent K_ε upper-bound formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: For every positive real number ε, there exists a constant K_ε such that for all triples (a, b, c) of coprime positive integers with a + b = c: c < K_ε · rad(abc)^{1+ε}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is logically equivalent to the ε-finiteness statement and is often used in discussions that require an explicit multiplicative constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little-o reformulation
rubrics_metrics.description: For all triples (a, b, c) of coprime positive integers with a + b = c, rad(abc) is at least c^{1-o(1)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recasts the conjecture in asymptotic little-o notation emphasizing that rad(abc) should grow nearly linearly with c (up to subpolynomial factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality q(a,b,c) definition and q-formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality q(a,b,c) of the triple (a,b,c) is defined as q(a,b,c) = log(c) / log(rad(abc)). The conjecture: for every ε>0 there are only finitely many coprime triples with a + b = c such that q(a,b,c) > 1 + ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: q(4,127,131)=0.46820..., q(3,125,128)=1.426565...; the article notes there are infinitely many triples with q>1 but conjectures only finitely many with q>1+ε for any fixed ε>0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of ε>0 (counterexample families)
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition ε>0 is necessary because there exist infinitely many triples with c > rad(abc); explicit families are given, e.g. a=1, b=2^{6n}-1, c=2^{6n} (n>1) showing rad(abc) < (2/3)c and more general constructions producing rad(abc) arbitrarily small compared to c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives the calculations that demonstrate these infinite families, showing why the conjecture must allow a positive ε to avoid trivial infinite counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of highest-quality triples and notion of 'quality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of triples with particularly small radical relative to c; the highest-known quality in the table is 1.6299 (example a=2, b=3^{10}·109, c=23^{5}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article includes a ranked table of highest-quality triples and notes that a triple achieving the maximal possible quality (if finite) must exist if the conjecture is true. The note refers back to the definition of quality q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of abc
rubrics_metrics.description: If true, the abc conjecture implies numerous results and conjectures in number theory, including Roth's theorem, Mordell (Faltings' theorem), Vojta's conjecture in dimension 1, Erdős–Woods conjecture (up to finitely many exceptions), infinitely many non-Wieferich primes in every base, weak forms of Marshall Hall's conjecture, Fermat's Last Theorem for n ≥ 6 (via an effective weak form), Fermat–Catalan, bounds on L-functions (no Siegel zero) under number-field versions, finiteness results about perfect powers of polynomials, generalizations of Tijdeman's theorem, and implications for Beal's conjecture and Lang's conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents this as a large, non-exhaustive list of important consequences and conditional proofs that would follow from various forms of abc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proven theoretical upper bounds relating c and rad(abc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Known unconditional bounds showing c can be bounded above in terms of rad(abc) by exponential functions, e.g. c < exp(K1 · rad(abc)^{15}) (Stewart & Tijdeman 1986), c < exp(K2 · rad(abc)^{2/3+ε}) (Stewart & Yu 1991), and c < exp(K3 · rad(abc)^{1/3}(log rad(abc))^3) (Stewart & Yu 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constants K1, K3 are absolute; K2 depends effectively on ε. These results are far weaker than the conjectured near-linear relation, but are rigorous partial results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower-bound/obstruction results to extremely strong forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Results showing there are infinitely many triples with c > rad(abc) · exp(k sqrt(log c)/log log c) for certain k (Stewart & Tijdeman 1986; van Frankenhuysen improved k), demonstrating lower bounds on how strong any abc-type inequality can be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theoretical results give constraints on the possible strength of any abc statement and are cited to show limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational project and distribution data (ABC@Home)
rubrics_metrics.description: ABC@Home is a distributed computing project launched to discover triples (a,b,c) with rad(abc) < c and to study patterns; as of May 2014 it had found 23.8 million triples. The article includes a table of counts of triples with q>1, q>1.05, etc., for ranges c < 10^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This computational data is presented as empirical evidence and a resource for studying the distribution of high-quality triples; it cannot resolve the conjecture but may offer insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined forms, explicit conjectures and generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger or alternative conjectures are described: Baker's strengthening replacing rad(abc) by ε^{-ω} rad(abc) (ω = number of distinct primes dividing a,b,c); Baker's explicit abc (c < κ rad(abc) (log rad(abc))^{ω}/ω! with κ absolute); Granville's variants involving K^{Ω(abc)} rad(abc); Robert–Stewart–Tenenbaum precise asymptotic conjectures; and the n-conjecture generalizing to n>2 integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These refinements propose sharper bounds or alternate multiplicative/logarithmic factors and are discussed with their motivating heuristics and computational experiments (e.g., Baker's choice of κ≈6/5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and standards for claimed proofs (Mochizuki and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical account of claimed proofs: Szpiro (2007) proposed a solution later found incorrect; Shinichi Mochizuki has claimed a proof via inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUTT) since 2012, with sustained controversy: long/difficult papers, at least one alleged gap identified by Scholze & Stix, some supporters and workshops, and publication in RIMS (2021) with continued skepticism in the wider community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that broad acceptance by the mathematical community, identification and resolution of gaps, and clear communication and verification by experts are the standards for accepting a claimed proof; it documents the debate and the reasons for continued doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational distribution of qualities q>1 by bound on c
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabulated counts of triples with q>1 and stricter thresholds (q>1.05, q>1.1, etc.) for ranges c < 10^2, 10^3, ..., 10^18 are provided to show empirical frequency of high-quality triples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table demonstrates how the number of high-quality triples grows with search bound and gives concrete data points (e.g., counts for c < 10^6, 10^9, etc.). This supports empirical study but not a proof.
